title: Little Manhattan
full_review:
When it comes to heart, the modest-sized "Little Manhattan" (20th Century Fox) comes up big.

Directed by Mark Levin (from a script written by his wife, Jennifer Flackett), the tender tale of first love is a warm and wonderful film that could be one of this year's surprise hits.

Set against a picturesque New York City backdrop, the story gently orbits around 10-year-old Gabe Burton (Josh Hutcherson), whose summer vacation is blissfully spent shooting hoops with his buddies and darting around his neighborhood on his scooter.

His devoted parents -- Adam (Bradley Whitford) and Leslie (Cynthia Nixon) -- are in the process of a protracted, if amicable, divorce, yet are still living under the same roof.

Like most boys his age, Gabe is firm in his belief that girls are "gross" and can, through even the slightest touch, transmit the dreaded schoolyard malady known as cooties.

That is until apple-cheeked Rosemary Telesco (Charlie Ray) walks into his karate class. The instructor pairs them off as sparring partners. Gabe falls hard, figuratively and literally. In that New York minute, everything changes.

Gabe suddenly finds himself tongue-tied around Rosemary. He stakes out her lobby in the hopes of "coincidentally" bumping into her -- which he does, leading to his first "official" date (a nonchaperoned stroll through Central Park).

But, just when he discovers he has a heart, Gabe gets it broken when Rosemary tells him that she will be leaving for camp, and possibly transferring to a private school come autumn.

Funny, charming and universal in its appeal, "Little Manhattan" radiates a disarming innocence, affectionately navigating Gabe's agony and ecstasy from his child-size perspective and avoiding the cynicism that maturity can sometimes bring.
The bittersweet ending is sentimental without overdoing it.

The young leads are endearing. And the romantic Big Apple scenery provides the perfect canvas for puppy love to bloom.

Levin, who wrote for the television series "The Wonder Years," uses similar voiceover narration here to good effect.

As family entertainment goes, "Little Manhattan" can go a long way. It conveys both the giddy highs and maddening lows of first love, as well as its accompanying confusion, anxiety, awkwardness, and ultimately its magic.

The film contains some minor thematic elements, schoolyard fisticuffs, mild rude language and an instance of vomit humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
